clinicalPearls: A left-dominant form of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy in which fibrofatty replacement predominantly affects the left ventricle, often the subepicardial and mid-wall inferolateral regions, with relatively preserved right ventricular function

Frequently caused by variants in desmosomal genes, especially desmoplakin (DSP), and in the non-desmosomal gene filamin C (FLNC); inheritance is usually autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance and variable expression
Ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death can occur early and out of proportion to the degree of systolic dysfunction, sometimes before overt cardiomyopathy is apparent
Patients may present with palpitations, syncope, chest pain mimicking myocarditis, or 'hot phases' of myocardial inflammation with troponin release and normal coronary arteries

The resting ECG may show lateral or inferolateral T-wave inversion, low QRS voltages in the limb leads, and ventricular ectopy of right bundle branch block morphology reflecting left ventricular origin
Cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement is central to diagnosis, typically demonstrating a subepicardial or mid-wall ring-like pattern of left ventricular scar

Because arrhythmic risk is not fully predicted by ejection fraction, risk stratification for an implantable defibrillator relies on genotype, extent of scar, arrhythmia burden, syncope, and family history
First-degree relatives should be offered cascade genetic testing and periodic clinical, ECG, and imaging surveillance
reference.pathophysiology: The condition arises from impaired mechanical coupling and structural integrity of cardiomyocytes, most often due to pathogenic variants in desmosomal proteins such as desmoplakin or in the cytoskeletal protein filamin C. Weakened cell-cell adhesion and disturbed signalling promote cardiomyocyte death, inflammation, and progressive replacement of myocardium by fibrous and fatty tissue. In the left-dominant pattern this fibrofatty scarring concentrates in the left ventricular subepicardium and mid-wall, creating a substrate for re-entrant ventricular arrhythmias while systolic function may remain relatively preserved until late. Episodic myocardial inflammation ('hot phases') can accelerate injury and mimic myocarditis.
additionalDifferentials: Classic right-dominant arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy
Dilated cardiomyopathy of other genetic or acquired cause
Idiopathic ventricular arrhythmia in a structurally normal heart
Ischaemic scar from prior myocardial infarction
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG looking for inferolateral T-wave inversion, low limb-lead voltages, and ventricular ectopy
Cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement to define left ventricular subepicardial and mid-wall scar
Ambulatory and exercise ECG monitoring to quantify ventricular arrhythmia burden
Transthoracic echocardiography to assess biventricular size and function
Genetic testing of an arrhythmogenic and dilated cardiomyopathy gene panel with cascade screening of relatives
Signal-averaged ECG and, in selected cases, electrophysiological or endomyocardial evaluation
redFlags: Syncope, aborted sudden death, or sustained ventricular tachycardia
Family history of sudden cardiac death, especially at a young age
Rapidly progressive heart failure or biventricular involvement
High-risk genotype such as desmoplakin or filamin C truncating variants with extensive scar
Recurrent chest pain with troponin rise and unobstructed coronaries suggesting an inflammatory hot phase
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies widely: some carriers remain asymptomatic while others suffer life-threatening arrhythmia or progressive heart failure. Because sudden death may precede significant systolic impairment, prognosis is driven more by arrhythmic substrate and genotype than by ejection fraction alone, and appropriate defibrillator therapy and activity modification improve survival.
pitfalls: Labelling recurrent troponin-positive episodes as isolated myocarditis and missing the underlying inherited cardiomyopathy
Relying on ejection fraction alone for defibrillator decisions and underestimating arrhythmic risk
Overlooking the diagnosis because the right ventricle appears normal on echocardiography
Failing to arrange cardiac MRI, which may be the only test to reveal the characteristic subepicardial scar
Not offering cascade genetic testing and surveillance to at-risk relatives
references: ESC Guidelines on the management of cardiomyopathies
GeneReviews: Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy and desmosomal disease
management: Restrict high-intensity and endurance exercise, which accelerates fibrofatty progression and provokes ventricular arrhythmia
Beta-blockade as baseline antiarrhythmic therapy, adding agents such as sotalol or amiodarone for ventricular arrhythmia suppression
Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for secondary prevention after sustained ventricular tachycardia or aborted arrest, and for primary prevention in high-risk desmoplakin or filamin C genotypes
Catheter ablation for recurrent ventricular tachycardia refractory to drug therapy
Guideline-directed heart failure therapy with neurohormonal blockade once left ventricular systolic dysfunction develops
Recognise and manage inflammatory hot phases, monitoring troponin and differentiating them from acute myocarditis
Surveillance with serial ECG, ambulatory monitoring and cardiac MRI to track arrhythmic burden and scar progression
Offer genetic testing and counselling for this autosomal dominant condition, with cascade screening of relatives and advanced heart failure referral for transplant assessment when refractory
